_source: Standard culinary technique. Temperatures are stated as cooking targets; where a target is below the FDA's 145°F guideline for finfish, the page says so explicitly. No claims here are attributed to Brandywine.

methods.name: Grilling
methods.one_line: Direct high heat over open flame, best on firm fish thick enough to survive being turned.
methods.gear: Charcoal or gas grill, a well-scraped and oiled grate, a thin metal spatula
methods.technique: Get the grate ripping hot and clean it twice. Oil the fish, not the grate — oil on hot bars burns before the fish lands. Put the fish down and leave it alone; it releases on its own when a crust forms, usually three to four minutes. If it sticks, it is not ready to turn.
methods.timing: Roughly 8–10 minutes per inch of thickness, total, turned once.
methods.suits: Firm, thick, and ideally fatty. Fat drips, flares, and bastes.
methods.avoid: Thin delicate fillets — sole, small rockfish — fall through and fall apart.
methods.mistake: Turning too early. Nearly every piece of fish that tears on a grill was moved before it had released.
methods.skin: Skin-on, skin-side down first, and leave it there for two-thirds of the total time. The skin is a heat shield.
methods.doneness: Pull 5°F below your target — carryover finishes it while it rests.

methods.name: Pan-Searing
methods.one_line: A hot heavy pan and very little movement — the most reliable way to cook nearly anything in the case.
methods.gear: Cast iron or heavy stainless. Not nonstick — it will not build the crust.
methods.technique: Dry the fish completely with paper towel; surface water is the enemy of a crust. Salt just before it goes in, not earlier. Lay it away from you, press it flat for ten seconds so it does not curl, then leave it. Turn once.
methods.timing: About 4 minutes on the first side, 1–2 on the second, for a one-inch fillet.
methods.suits: Almost everything. It is the default technique for a reason.
methods.avoid: Nothing, though very thick cuts are better started in the pan and finished in the oven.
methods.mistake: A wet fillet and a cold pan. Together they produce grey steamed fish with no crust at all.
methods.skin: Skin-side down, pressed flat, 80% of the cooking time. Done right, the skin is the best part.
methods.doneness: The crust tells you about the pan; a thermometer tells you about the fish. Use both.

methods.name: Roasting
methods.one_line: Dry oven heat — the least demanding method and the easiest one to walk away from.
methods.heat: 400–425°F for fillets; 325°F for slow-roasting fatty fish
methods.gear: Sheet pan, parchment, an instant-read thermometer
methods.technique: Bring the fish to room temperature for fifteen minutes first so it cooks evenly. Oil, salt, and give it space — crowded fish steams. Slow-roasting at low heat is the single most forgiving way to cook a fatty fillet.
methods.timing: 10–12 minutes at 425°F for a one-inch fillet; 25–30 minutes at 325°F for a slow roast.
methods.suits: Whole fish, thick fillets, and anything fatty. Black cod slow-roasted is close to foolproof.
methods.avoid: Very thin fillets, which are done before they take on any color.
methods.mistake: Cooking by the clock instead of by temperature. Oven thermostats lie by 25°F in both directions.
methods.skin: Skin-side down on the pan. It will not crisp; that is not what roasting is for.
methods.doneness: Probe the thickest part. Fish keeps climbing 3–5°F out of the oven.

methods.name: Smoking
methods.one_line: Low heat and wood smoke over hours — a preservation method that turned into a delicacy.
methods.gear: A smoker or a grill set up for indirect heat, alder or applewood, a probe thermometer
methods.technique: Brine first — a basic cure of salt and sugar, four to twelve hours depending on thickness. Rinse, then air-dry on a rack in the fridge until the surface turns tacky. That tacky layer, the pellicle, is what smoke actually sticks to; skip it and the smoke rolls off.
methods.timing: 2–4 hours hot-smoked, depending on thickness and how heavily you want it flavored.
methods.suits: Fatty fish above all — salmon, steelhead, black cod, albacore. Fat carries smoke.
methods.avoid: Very lean white fish, which dries out long before it takes on flavor.
methods.mistake: Skipping the pellicle. It is the difference between smoked fish and fish that sat near some smoke.
methods.wood: Brandywine's own smoked line is applewood and alderwood — alder is the traditional Pacific Northwest wood for salmon.

methods.name: Poaching
methods.one_line: Gentle submersion in barely-moving liquid — the most controlled and least forgiving-of-neglect method.
methods.heat: Liquid held at 160–180°F. It should never boil, barely shiver.
methods.gear: A wide shallow pan, enough liquid to just cover, a thermometer
methods.technique: Court bouillon — water with wine, aromatics, and salt — or olive oil for a richer result. Slide the fish in, hold the temperature, and do not let it come to a boil. Boiling liquid shreds fish.
methods.suits: Lean, delicate fish that would dry out anywhere else, and anything you want to serve cold later.
methods.avoid: Nothing, though it produces no crust, so it is the wrong choice when you want texture.
methods.mistake: Letting the liquid boil. The moment it rolls, the fish starts falling apart.
methods.skin: Skin off — it goes flabby and unpleasant in liquid.
methods.doneness: The fish turns opaque and just yields to a fork. It happens fast at the end.

methods.name: Frying
methods.one_line: Hot oil and a coating — the treatment most of the lean white fish in the case eventually gets.
methods.gear: A heavy pot filled no more than a third, a clip thermometer, a wire rack
methods.technique: Dry the fish, then flour, then batter. Fry in small batches — every piece you add drops the oil temperature, and oil below 325°F soaks in instead of crisping. Let it recover between batches. Drain on a rack, never on paper, which steams the underside soft.
methods.timing: 3–5 minutes depending on thickness, until deep golden.
methods.suits: Lean white fish. Rockfish, cod, lingcod — this is what fish and chips is made of.
methods.avoid: Fatty fish like black cod, which turns greasy on greasy.
methods.mistake: Crowding the pot. It is the single most common frying error and it makes everything soggy.
methods.batter: Cold beer batter, mixed at the last second and left lumpy. Overmixing develops gluten and turns the crust tough.
methods.doneness: Golden and floating. Fish fries fast.

methods.name: Serving Raw
methods.one_line: Crudo, sashimi, ceviche and poke — where handling quality is the entire dish.
methods.gear: A genuinely sharp knife, a cold board, cold plates
methods.technique: Slice against the grain at an angle, in one draw of the blade — sawing tears the muscle and ruins the surface. Keep everything cold, work quickly, dress it right before it goes out.
methods.timing: Served immediately. Ceviche is the exception: 15–30 minutes in citrus firms the outside while the center stays tender.
methods.suits: Tuna above all, and salmon. This is the category where Brandywine's never-frozen, iced-on-the-boat handling is the whole argument — their own site calls it "Sushi Grade".
methods.avoid: Lean white bottom fish, and anything you are not confident about the handling of.
methods.mistake: A dull knife. It crushes rather than cuts and the texture goes to mush.
methods.safety: Raw fish is a handling question, not a species question — buy it from a counter that can tell you when it landed, keep it cold, and eat it the same day. Standard public-health guidance is that pregnant people, young children, older adults and anyone immunocompromised should avoid raw fish entirely.
methods.doneness: Not applicable — but temperature is. It should be cold when it reaches the plate.

methods.name: Steaming
methods.one_line: Moist heat in a covered pot — the method shellfish is built for.
methods.heat: An inch of hard-boiling liquid under a tight lid
methods.gear: A wide pot with a lid that actually seals
methods.technique: Get the liquid boiling hard before anything goes in — wine, beer, or water with aromatics. Add the shellfish, cover, and leave the lid on. Every time you lift it you lose the steam and add minutes.
methods.timing: 3–5 minutes for mussels, 5–7 for clams, until the shells open.
methods.suits: Mussels, clams, crab, shrimp. Whole fish, if you have a pot big enough.
methods.avoid: Anything you want browned. Steam and crust are mutually exclusive.
methods.mistake: Cooking until every last shell opens. The stubborn few are dead ones — discard them rather than steaming the rest into rubber waiting.
methods.liquid: The liquid left in the pot is the best part. Bread, and do not throw it out.
methods.doneness: Shells open. That is the signal, and it is a reliable one.
